articles.title: Viatura da PM é arrastada por enxurrada em Araçoiaba da Serra | G1
articles.standfirst: Policiais estavam a caminho de atendimento quando tiveram a viatura empurrada pela força da correnteza que inundou o bairro Campo do Meio.
articles.summary: Policiais militares foram resgatados com ferimentos leves após a viatura ser arrastada por uma forte enxurrada no bairro Campo do Meio, em Araçoiaba da Serra.
articles.body:
Viatura da PM fica presa em enchente em Araçoiaba da Serra — Foto: Defesa Civil / Divulgação

Uma equipe da Polícia Militar (PM) precisou ser resgatada após ter a viatura arrastada por uma enchente no bairro Campo do Meio, em Araçoiaba da Serra (SP), durante a chuva da madrugada deste domingo (25).

Os policiais conseguiram sair do veículo e foram encaminhados ao Pronto Atendimento com escoriações leves. A Defesa Civil atendeu a ocorrência e ajudou a recuperar os pertences que ficaram dentro do veículo.

A equipe da PM estava em direção a um atendimento, por volta das 3h, quando, ao passar por um trecho de ponte na Alameda Itapetininga, a viatura foi arrastada pela força da água e acabou presa entre galhos e um poste de energia elétrica.

A Defesa Civil foi ao local para apoiar a recuperação da viatura e os pertences dos policiais. A remoção da viatura foi feita somente horas depois, após a diminuição do nível da água.

Em Sorocaba (SP) houve registros de alagamentos, interdições de vias e queda de muro. Um dos principais impactos foi a cheia do Rio Sorocaba, que levou à interdição da Avenida Dom Aguirre, nas proximidades da Praça Lions e do bairro Santa Rosália; da avenida Juvenal de Campos; e da rua Saliba Mota, por conta do avanço da água.

Segundo a Defesa Civil, a maior rajada de vento registrada em Sorocaba nas últimas 24 horas foi de 25 km/h, entre 2h e 3h da madrugada deste domingo. Choveu 84 milímetros em 12 horas na cidade, sendo 40,2 milímetros somente em quatro horas.

Avenida Dom Aguirre ficou inundada após as chuvas da madrugada em Sorocaba (SP) — Foto: Reprodução / TV TEM

Duas jovens morreram arrastadas pela correnteza de uma enchente na madrugada deste domingo (25), em Jundiaí (SP). Vídeos mostram o momento que outras pessoas se arriscam na enxurrada ao tentarem atravessar a rua na saída de um clube no bairro Casa Branca. As vítimas são Rhaynny Rodrigues da Silva Barbosa, de 19 anos, e Laura Raianny Pereira da Silva, de 16 anos.

O Corpo de Bombeiros foi acionado para localizar e socorrer as vítimas por volta das 5h. Uma das mulheres chegou a ser encaminhada ao Hospital de Caridade São Vicente de Paulo, mas não resistiu. A outra mulher teve a morte constatada no local pela equipe dos bombeiros. O corpo dela foi encontrado em um córrego.

articles.summary: Caso aconteceu no bairro Campo Belo.
articles.body:
Hospital Municipal da Japuíba, em Angra dos Reis. — Foto: Divulgação/Secretaria Executiva de Comunicação de Angra dos Reis

Um acidente entre um carro e uma moto deixou um homem ferido neste domingo (25) em Angra dos reis (RJ). O caso aconteceu no bairro Campo Belo.

Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, o acionamento aconteceu para o atendimento na Rua H.

Ainda de acordo com a corporação, o ferido, que conduzia a motocicleta, foi encaminhado para o Hospital Municipal da Japuíba.

O g1 entrou em contato com a unidade médica para atualizar o estado de saúde da vítima, mas não obteve retorno.

Até o momento da publicação desta reportagem a dinâmica do acidente era desconhecida.

articles.title: Eight birds glued to sticks in 'horrific incident' in Wickford
articles.summary: A wildlife charity founder says it has left her "heartbroken, frustrated and angry".
articles.body:
The discovery of eight birds glued to wooden sticks has left the founder of a wildlife charity "heartbroken, frustrated and angry".

Sue Schwar from the South Essex Wildlife Hospital in Orsett said a member of the public spotted a blue tit struggling near a makeshift bird feeding station in Wickford that had been surrounded by glue-coated wooden dowels.

She said six blue tits and two great tits were taken to their hospital for treatment on Thursday and were expected to make a full recovery.

The charity confirmed it was working with Essex Police and the RSPCA as part of an investigation into the "truly horrific incident".

In a Facebook post, it said: "Missing feathers, bruising and significant stress plagued every single one of them but, amazingly, they seem to be doing well in our care."

Two volunteers were sent to the scene after the incident was reported.

Schwar said the birds were "lucky to have been found".

"I'm heartbroken, frustrated, really angry that we have to deal with wildlife crimes, like this, almost on a daily basis."

All the glue has now been removed from the animals but she expects it to be "weeks" before they are released back into the wild, as their feathers need to grow back and become weatherproof again.

articles.title: Catholic alcohol consumption drops to record low as Americans rethink moderate drinking habits
articles.summary: Catholic adults now report drinking rates near the levels of Protestants as shifting health views and social habits reshape moderate drinking in America.
articles.body: A historic shift in American drinking habits shows Catholic alcohol consumption reaching record lows, though scientific experts caution against attributing the drop strictly to religious or cultural changes. The share of Catholic adults in the United States who report drinking alcohol has fallen to 55%, according to a Gallup report authored by analyst Frank Newport. That marks a decline from the 2002–2004 period, when 79% of Catholics reported consuming alcoholic beverages. Over that same timeframe, self-reported Protestant drinking rates remained flat at 54%. HEAVY DRINKING SURGES AMONG AMERICANS IN ONE AGE GROUP AS OTHER GENERATIONS CUT BACK "Drinking has dropped significantly within both the group of those who have no religious identity and, in particular, among Catholics," Newport wrote in the analysis. However, experts urged caution when drawing sweeping conclusions from subgroup survey data. Dr. Joshua Gowin, an associate professor in the Department of Radiology at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus who studies alcohol's effects on the brain, noted that self-reported polling figures can fluctuate based on sampling. "There's definitely a general pattern of alcohol use decreasing across groups," Gowin told Fox News Digital. "As far as the subgroups go, it wasn't clear or necessarily compelling to me that one group was showing a broad trend that wasn't reflected in the other groups," he went on. BRAD PITT SAYS HE CAN DRINK IN ‘RESTRAINED MANNER’ AFTER 7 SOBER YEARS, BUT EXPERT RAISES RED FLAG "It seemed like really only one data point showed that effect ... which made me a little skeptical that this is a broader phenomenon versus a single survey sample." Despite methodological limitations in tracking specific religious subgroups, researchers agree that broader social and health trends are driving a shift in overall drinking habits. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Gallup findings indicate that a majority of Americans now view moderate drinking — defined as one or two drinks per day — as bad for their health. In the latest polling, 52% of Catholics said moderate alcohol consumption is bad for health, alongside 56% of adults with no religious affiliation and 48% of Protestants. Gowin noted that this public shift reflects decades of neuroscience and medical research. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "Twenty years ago, there was still kind of a push and pull between some benefits of alcohol and then some things that even then we knew were potentially harmful," he said. "It's not like the serious problems have gone away." "Over time, we've gotten a lot more clarity on the things that are bad for our health ... the balance has just shifted more in favor of the evidence for negative health effects." Gowin pointed out that large-scale neuroimaging studies now consistently link higher alcohol consumption to reduced brain volume, reinforcing public health warnings. Researchers also attribute shifting consumption patterns to broader societal changes, including shifts in social behavior and loneliness. Much of America's alcohol consumption has historically occurred in group settings, and changes in how people gather socially may be influencing drinking habits, they believe. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ At the same time, experts caution that a drop in general social drinking does not mean severe alcohol problems have dissolved. "One of the things that is a bit of a contradiction ... is that although the overall prevalence among all adults is down for the number of drinkers, there is actually a larger number of alcohol-related deaths in the past few years," Gowin noted. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's not like the serious problems have gone away."

articles.title: ‘Grabbed hair, pinned to ground, tore shirt’: Patient attacks doctor, hospital staff in Punjab
articles.summary: MOHALI: A patient at a sub-divisional hospital in Kharar, Punjab's Mohali, allegedly assaulted a medical officer by grabbing her hair, pinning her to the
articles.body: MOHALI: A patient at a sub-divisional hospital in Kharar, Punjab's Mohali, allegedly assaulted a medical officer by grabbing her hair, pinning her to the ground and tearing her shirt, police said on Sunday.The incident took place on Saturday night when the accused, identified as Rajatpal Singh, a resident of Kharar, allegedly turned aggressive and attacked the doctor and other medical staff members. He also allegedly vandalised hospital property, police said.Singh was subsequently arrested. Hospital staff managed to subdue him following the alleged assault.According to a hospital staff member, the doctor and a nurse approached Singh to provide treatment when he allegedly became violent and attacked them.Police registered a case at Kharar police station based on the doctor's complaint under relevant sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), including Sections 115 (2) (voluntary hurt), 132 (assaulting a public servant) and 221 (obstructing a public servant in the discharge of public functions). The case was also registered under the Public Property Prevention of Damage Act.The Punjab Civil Medical Services Association (PCMSA) condemned the incident and demanded a proper security framework for doctors.In a statement issued on Sunday, PCMSA president Dr Akhil Sareen said the association had received a representation regarding the incident.The association said there were allegedly no security arrangements at the hospital when the attack took place, triggering outrage among members of the PCMS cadre.The PCMSA also reiterated its demand for the deployment of 287 security guards at sub-divisional hospitals across Punjab. It said the proposal was at an advanced stage of consideration at the Punjab Health Systems Corporation (PHSC) and should be implemented without further delay.The association has set November 12 as the deadline for implementing Phase II of the security framework, which aims to enhance safety at all sub-divisional hospitals across Punjab.(With Agency Inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chandigarh | Silver Rate in Chandigarh | Bank Holidays in Chandigarh | Public Holidays in Chandigarh | Chandigarh AQI | Weather in Chandigarh | Petrol Price in Chandigarh | Diesel Price in Chandigarh | CNG Price in Chandigarh | LPG Price in ChandigarhStay updated with the latest Chandigarh news. articles.title: Seven killed in Gaza as Israel targets university campus and other sites
articles.summary: Israeli air strike kills three security guards in one of two attacks on the Islamic University in Gaza City.
articles.body:
At least seven Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks across Gaza, including one that targeted a university campus in Gaza City.

Three security guards were killed in an Israeli air strike on the Islamic University campus on Sunday, the second attack that targeted the institution in the space of a few hours.

Reporting from the scene immediately after the attack, Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud said, “The aftermath was massive.”

“The bloodstains, the pieces of flesh of the bodies that were torn apart were on the ground; the smell of the acrid, burning concrete mixed with the flesh and the blood,” Mahmoud added, saying that the Al Jazeera team had just finished filming on site and greeted the three security guards before the strike killed them.

“We could hear the hissing sound of flying shrapnel everywhere to the point we thought we were going to be hit,” our correspondent said.

In the earlier drone strike on the campus, seven female students were injured by flying shrapnel.

“One of them was seriously injured and was transferred to a nearby field hospital,” Mahmoud said.

Separately, in southern Gaza, the Nasser Medical Complex reported that two people were killed as a result of Israeli shelling in al-Mawasi in Khan Younis. Several people were also wounded, including a child.

A person was also killed in an Israeli drone strike east of Deir el-Balah in central Gaza, and another person was killed, and several others wounded, in an attack on al-Rashid Street, near Hamad Hospital in the northern Gaza Strip, the Palestinian Wafa news agency reported.

The Popular Resistance Committees in Palestine condemned the university attacks, calling on mediators and international guarantors to step in to stop Israeli violations.

According to the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, UNESCO, nearly 95 percent of Gaza’s higher education campuses have been destroyed or damaged since Israel’s genocidal war began in October 2023.

Mahmoud noted that the majority of buildings at the Islamic University were already destroyed before Sunday’s attacks. “Only a couple of these buildings are partially standing,” he said.

The incident is “a reminder that a sense of security is painfully out of reach, even inside the place where students are supposed to be learning without the fear of these attacks”, he added.

The latest figures released by the Palestinian Ministry of Health in Gaza show that at least 1,551 people have been killed since the “ceasefire” began in October 2025, and 5,573 have been injured.

The total death toll from Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip is 74,544, with at least 175,692 people wounded since October 2023.

Israel also continues to occupy more and more land inside the Strip, with almost two-thirds of Gaza now under Israel’s military control or subject to its restrictions.

Palestinians there are also experiencing an escalating food crisis as a result of ongoing Israeli crossing closures and reduced international funding for assistance.

articles.title: Man held for hacking wife to death, burying body in house
articles.summary: Jamshedpur: Man arrested for allegedly killing his wife with an axe after a dinner argument and burying her body under their house floor in West Singhbhum.
articles.body: Jamshedpur: A 49-year-old man was arrested on Sunday for allegedly hacking his wife to death and burying her body inside their house at Tungi village in West Singhbhum district, police said.The accused, Ram Hansda, allegedly attacked his wife, Guruwari Hansda (47), with an axe on Oct 17 after an argument over dinner, in what police described as a fit of rage. Investigators said he dug a pit inside the house and buried the body to conceal the crime and delay detection by neighbours.Guruwari had not been seen in the village since Oct 17. After she remained untraceable for several days, neighbours grew suspicious and informed her married daughters. One of them, Nagisri Gagrai (30), reached Tungi on Saturday from Kharsawan in neighbouring Seraikela-Kharsawan district, where she lives with her in-laws.Police said family members inspected the house and noticed dried bloodstains on the interior walls. They then informed Pandrashali police outpost, and a team reached the village and began an inquiry.During questioning of locals and a preliminary probe, police learnt that Guruwari’s body had allegedly been buried under the floor of the house. Officers said the burial appeared aimed at destroying evidence and preventing immediate detection by villagers living nearby. After completing administrative formalities, police excavated the spot in the presence of a magistrate.“The decomposed body of the woman was recovered from the pit on Saturday,” a police officer said.Police took custody of the body and sent it to Sadar Hospital in Chaibasa for post-mortem examination after completing the necessary formalities.ASP Raj Kumar Jayaraju said an FIR was registered on the basis of Nagisri’s complaint. Hansda was arrested on Sunday and remanded in judicial custody. Jayaraju said the accused allegedly confessed during questioning. Police also recovered the axe allegedly used in the murder.Police said further investigation is under way to establish the sequence of events and corroborate the confession with forensic and post-mortem findings.Stay updated with the latest Ranchi news. articles.title: Chennai bus-motorcycle collision injures three teens, driver assaulted
articles.summary: Chennai: Three 17-year-olds hurt in Ennore bus-motorcycle crash near Thazhankuppam; MTC driver assaulted, bus stoned, police probe cause.
articles.body: Three minor boys sustained serious leg injuries after their motorcycle collided with an MTC bus at Thazhankuppam in Ennore on Saturday night.Police said, the boys, aged 17 and residents of Nettukuppam in Ennore, were returning home after playing kabaddi and were travelling on the same motorcycle. The boys tried to overtake the bus near Thazhankuppam when their motorcycle collided with it. All three sustained serious injuries to their legs. The bus was driven by Srinivasan, a resident of Ponneri.Residents gathered at the spot and assaulted Srinivasan. Some of them also pelted stones at the bus, damaging its front windshield. On receiving information, police rushed to the spot and brought the situation under control. The injured boys were taken to a nearby private hospital. articles.title: Selena Gomez's vaping admission highlights hidden health risks doctors say millions face daily
articles.summary: Selena Gomez called vaping "stupid" after it altered her voice, but doctors warn the health risks go beyond vocal cord damage for millions.
articles.body: When Selena Gomez revealed to her millions of followers that heavy nicotine vaping had noticeably altered her voice, calling the habit "stupid," her confession highlighted a larger issue with the practice. For the singer and actress, the physical toll manifested in her vocal cords. But medical professionals emphasize that her experience is only a visible symptom of a deeper health crisis affecting millions of Americans who use e-cigarettes every day. While often marketed as a safer alternative to conventional cigarettes, e-cigarettes pose significant health risks. Aside from the immediate vocal strain and airway inflammation noted by otolaryngologists, major health institutions warn that regular vaping exposes the body to a cocktail of toxic chemicals, cardiovascular strain and respiratory risks. SELENA GOMEZ WARNS FANS AFTER VAPING HABIT LEAVES HER WITH PERMANENT CONSEQUENCE Specialists emphasize that e-cigarettes deliver more concentrated doses of nicotine than traditional cigarettes, rapidly driving chemical dependency in the brain. "With e-cigarettes and vaping, you can get a very high dose of nicotine, and that directly correlates to addiction and how difficult it can be to break these patterns," Trent Carter, a nurse practitioner and CEO of Renew Health in New Mexico, previously told Fox News Digital. Carter notes that high nicotine intake without traditional smoke can carry its own health consequences. "It can lead to sleep disturbances, increased anxiety, and if you have underlying cardiac problems or high blood pressure, it’s going to raise your heart rate and elevate your blood pressure, leading to all sorts of issues." According to the American Lung Association, the aerosol produced by e-cigarettes contains fine chemical particles, heavy metals such as nickel and lead, and organic compounds. Over time, inhaling these irritants can trigger chronic airway inflammation, irreversible lung tissue scarring, and obstructive pulmonary conditions. NEVER SMOKED A CIGARETTE? YOU COULD STILL BE AT HIGHER RISK FOR LUNG CANCER A major concern among physicians is the chemical composition of e-liquids. Even nicotine-free formulas contain flavorings and solvent agents like propylene glycol and vegetable glycerin. When heated by the device’s coil, these liquids break down into toxic compounds, including formaldehyde and acrolein, both known to damage cellular structures in the respiratory system. Doctors stress that because modern e-cigarettes have only been widely used for a little over a decade, long-term health consequences are still unclear. While immediate effects may appear as hoarseness, coughing, or reduced athletic endurance, the larger impact poses risks to long-term vital organ function. For many attempting to quit vaping, traditional tools like nicotine patches or gum can fall short because they don't address the psychological habit. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "While a patch or gum can help with physical cravings, if you aren't addressing the behavioral aspect, you're missing a huge component," Carter said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "Vaping can become constant throughout the day. Subconsciously, you might not even realize how frequently you're doing it, or that you're using it to cope with underlying anxiety or lack of sleep." CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES For those inspired by Gomez, health professionals urge people to seek comprehensive support rather than simply switch nicotine delivery methods. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The goal shouldn't be to find another way to consume nicotine, it should be to treat the dependence itself," said Carter.

articles.title: Sharpen memory and fight brain fog with simple 60-second trick from a neurologist
articles.summary: Dr. Rhonda Voskuhl explains why crosswords and sudoku miss the mark for brain fog and which timed word games actually target verbal memory loss.
articles.body: Brain games, crosswords and math puzzles are often promoted as ways to sharpen memory, but neurologists warn that generic exercises may not address the specific cause of mental fog. Dr. Rhonda Voskuhl, a professor of neurology at UCLA and co-founder of Cleopatra RX in Los Angeles, says brain exercises only work if they target the specific mental function that is slowing down. "You can’t just do random cognitive exercises," Voskuhl told Fox News Digital at the Livelong Women’s Health Summit in New York City in September. "They’ve got to fit the problem." DOCTOR REVEALS '10-YEAR RULE' FOR EVALUATING BRAIN FOG AND DEMENTIA SYMPTOMS The problem, she said, is verbal memory. "Doing math is not going to help … You need an exercise that will help you with words." Mental fog — especially the kind triggered by midlife hormone changes during perimenopause and menopause — impacts very specific areas of the brain, according to Voskuhl. When estrogen levels drop, overall intelligence and basic logic remain completely normal. Instead, the brain takes a hit in two main areas: verbal memory (recalling names and words) and processing speed (thinking quickly under pressure), experts say. FORGETTING NAMES AND LOSING KEYS MAY SIGNAL SOMETHING OTHER THAN DEMENTIA Games like Sudoku and other number puzzles primarily exercise logic and math skills, so they may not improve word-recall difficulties. "It’s not a global problem with the brain," Voskuhl said. "It’s not global brain atrophy, but there are some regions on MRIs and research studies that show that the hippocampus, the memory area, will have some atrophies, some functional connection issues." To understand why word-based exercises may help, it is useful to distinguish between the following two stages of memory, experts say. DAILY EATING HABIT LINKED TO BETTER BRAIN HEALTH IN OLDER ADULTS, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS Brain fog typically affects retrieval, not encoding. The word or name is still stored safely in the memory, but the brain's search engine is running slowly. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Building a better brain workout To effectively target brain fog, Voskuhl says exercises need to focus on two things: finding words and working quickly. "It’s basically processing speed," she said. "So you need an exercise that is going to be something that makes you rush, makes you do it quickly." The following types of exercises target processing speed and active word recall. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Instead of using generic puzzle apps, Voskuhl recommends paying attention to where you stumble in daily life and picking games that match those challenges. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP People "know themselves," she said — "what they are bad at or what they used to be good at and now they’re not as good at ... Once you know those things, you should think about what kind of games [to play]. You can play around with different games. You can see if it pushes you."

articles.title: Patient drags night-shift doctor by hair in Kharar civil hospital, assaults her along with two staffers.
articles.summary: Night-shift doctor assaulted in Kharar civil hospital; patient dragged her by hair, attacked staff and damaged property. Police book suspect under BNS.
articles.body: Mohali: A patient allegedly dragged a doctor to the ground by her hair and assaulted two responding medical staffers during a night shift at Kharar’s civil hospital.As CCTV footage of this Saturday-night attack inside the emergency ward sparked renewed security concerns across Punjab facilities, police charged the suspect, Ranjitpal Singh, under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and the Prevention of Damage to Public Property ActDr Harsharanpreet Kaur stated in her police complaint that hospital workers had found Ranjitpal Singh groaning in pain on the floor outside the emergency ward staff room late at night and moved him to a minor operating theatre.An argument broke out during treatment and the doctor alleged that as she exited the room, the man grabbed her hair, pulled her to the ground, hit her, and tore her clothes. After bashing up a nurse and an ambulance driver who intervened to protect her, the man damaged the hospital property before other employees restrained him.Suspect Ranjitpal Singh’s family alleged he had suffered an adverse reaction to incorrect medication. the family also accused the doctor of medical negligence and verbal aggression.. but police said these claims remained unverified and subject to investigation.Sub-inspector Sukhwinder Singh of the Kharar City police station said cops had filed charges under BNS sections 115(2), 132, 221, and 76 (which deal with assault, injury, obstructing public servant, and attempt to disrobe a woman), alongside property damage statutes.Investigators are reviewing closed-circuit television footage to confirm the sequence of events.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chandigarh | Silver Rate in Chandigarh | Bank Holidays in Chandigarh | Public Holidays in Chandigarh | Chandigarh AQI | Weather in Chandigarh | Petrol Price in Chandigarh | Diesel Price in Chandigarh | CNG Price in Chandigarh | LPG Price in ChandigarhStay updated with the latest Chandigarh news. articles.title: Motociclista morre após colisão entre motos na Avenida dos Holandeses, em São Luís | G1
articles.standfirst: Acidente aconteceu na manhã desta segunda-feira (26), na região do Calhau. Segundo testemunhas, a vítima bateu em um poste após a colisão. Outro motociclista ficou ferido.
articles.summary: Acidente aconteceu na manhã desta segunda-feira (26), na região do Calhau. Segundo testemunhas, a vítima bateu em um poste após a colisão. Outro motociclista ficou ferido.
articles.body:
Um motociclista morreu após um acidente envolvendo duas motos, na manhã desta segunda-feira (26), na Avenida dos Holandeses, na região do Calhau, em São Luís . A colisão aconteceu em frente a uma concessionária de veículos.

A vítima foi identificada como Cledson Nunes Sousa. Segundo testemunhas, ele pilotava uma motocicleta quando houve uma colisão com outra moto. Com o impacto, Cledson acabou atingindo um poste.

A vítima sofreu uma lesão grave no pescoço e morreu no local. Uma equipe do Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu) foi acionada e confirmou o óbito.

O outro motociclista envolvido no acidente ficou ferido e foi encaminhado ao Hospital Municipal Djalma Marques, conhecido como Socorrão I, em São Luís. Até o momento, não há informações sobre o estado de saúde dele.

As circunstâncias do acidente ainda não foram esclarecidas.

articles.title: PM apreende 114 cápsulas após mulher dizer que foi dopada | G1
articles.standfirst: Ela passou mal e procurou atendimento no Hospital Santa Marcelina onde ficou internada. A mulher afirmou que foi forçada a engolir cápsulas com a droga.
articles.summary: Ela passou mal e procurou atendimento no Hospital Santa Marcelina onde ficou internada. A mulher afirmou que foi forçada a engolir cápsulas com a droga.
articles.body:
Cápsulas com cocaína apreendidas em casa em Itaquaquecetuba — Foto: Polícia Militar/Divulgação

A Polícia Militar apreendeu 114 cápsulas com cocaína em uma casa em Itaquaquecetuba , neste domingo (25), após uma mulher internada no Hospital Santa Marcelina relatar que foi forçada a engolir cápsulas com a droga.

Segundo a PM, a mulher afirmou que foi dopada e que pessoas introduziram drogas no corpo dela para uma viagem internacional. Depois de passar mal, ela deixou o imóvel onde estava e procurou atendimento médico.

Com base no relato da paciente, policiais fizeram buscas na casa, mas não encontraram as pessoas mencionadas por ela, segundo a corporação.

Na casa, a PM apreendeu 114 cápsulas. Após análise, o Instituto de Criminalística de Mogi das Cruzes constatou que os invólucros continham 850,34 gramas de cocaína.

A polícia também apreendeu uma mala com roupas e pertences pessoais, uma bolsa, um passaporte e um celular.

A mulher permaneceu internada no Hospital Santa Marcelina, sob escolta policial, porque ainda não havia expelido os objetos que, segundo ela, continham drogas. A ocorrência foi registrada na Polícia Civil.

articles.title: Avô é preso por esfaquear neto com autismo em briga de família  | G1
articles.standfirst: O crime ocorreu na casa da família em Palestina (SP). A vítima tentava defender a mãe das ameaças e intimidações do avô.
articles.summary: Um homem de 62 anos é suspeito de esfaquear o neto de 18 anos, com Transtorno do Espectro Autista (TEA), durante uma briga de família na manhã de domingo (25) em Palestina (SP).
articles.body:
Crime ocorreu na casa da família em Palestina (SP) — Foto: TV TEM / Kelly Borges

Um homem de 62 anos foi preso suspeito de esfaquear o neto de 18 anos, com Transtorno do Espectro Autista (TEA), durante uma briga de família na manhã de domingo (25) em Palestina (SP).

Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, a vítima foi atingida na cabeça e no braço no momento em que tentava defender sua mãe das ameaças do idoso.

O desentendimento começou quando o suspeito pediu que a filha, mãe do jovem, saísse da residência. Quando a mulher negou, o idoso usou a faca para fazer ameaças e tentar intimidá-la. Em seguida, o jovem interveio e foi esfaqueado pelo avô. Ele foi socorrido e encaminhado para o Pronto Atendimento de Palestina.

Conforme apurado pela TV TEM , a vítima teve duas perfurações profundas na cabeça e uma no braço. Devido ao ferimento, foi encaminhada para o Hospital de Base (HB) de São José do Rio Preto (SP).

O avô foi preso encaminhado à carceragem da Divisão Especializada de Investigações Criminais (DEIC). O caso foi registrado como violência doméstica e homicídio tentado.

Pronto Atendimento de Palestina (SP) — Foto: TV TEM / Kelly Borges

articles.title: Homem tetraplégico há nove anos recebe ajuda de equipe para votar  | G1
articles.standfirst: Cláudio dos Santos mora em Conceição do Coité e sofreu um acidente. Por falta de transporte, ele não conseguiu comparecer ao primeiro turno das eleições.
articles.summary: Cláudio dos Santos mora em Conceição do Coité e sofreu um acidente. Por falta de transporte, ele não conseguiu comparecer ao primeiro turno das eleições.
articles.body:
Homem tetraplégico há nove anos recebe ajuda de equipe de resgate para votar em Conceição do Coité — Foto: Brigada Águia Resgate

Um homem de 52 anos que ficou tetraplégico após um acidente de moto recebeu ajuda de uma equipe de resgate para votar no segundo turno das eleições, neste domingo (25), em Conceição do Coité , na região sisaleira da Bahia.

Cláudio Lopes dos Santos sofreu o acidente há nove anos e mora com a mãe, Ivonildes Lopes dos Santos. Segundo a equipe Águia Resgate, ele sente dores diariamente, o que dificulta a locomoção. Por falta de transporte, Cláudio não conseguiu comparecer às urnas no primeiro turno.

Diante da dificuldade, a mãe dele solicitou o apoio da equipe para levá-lo até a Universidade do Estado da Bahia (Uneb), onde ele vota.

Quatro socorristas participaram da ação, realizada por volta das 12h. A equipe aguardou Cláudio concluir a votação e, em seguida, fez o transporte dele de volta para casa.

O momento em que Cláudio chegou ao local de votação e exerceu o direito ao voto foi registrado em vídeo pela equipe de resgate.

Cláudio Lopes dos Santos conseguiu ajuda e votou em Conceição do Coité no segundo turno das eleições — Foto: Brigada Águia Resgate

De acordo com a Águia Resgate, essa foi a primeira vez que o grupo realizou uma iniciativa desse tipo.

Ao g1 , Ivonildes contou que o filho sofreu o acidente de moto em Conceição do Coité e ficou internado no Hospital Geral Clériston Andrade, em Feira de Santana . Segundo ela, ele conseguia falar normalmente após o acidente, mas, com o passar do tempo, passou a apresentar dificuldades na fala.

A mãe relatou que Cláudio ficou deprimido por não conseguir votar no primeiro turno. Para o segundo turno, ele manifestou novamente a vontade de participar da votação.

“Eu me comuniquei com uma pessoa para programar a ida dele, e o Águia foi buscar. Pessoas maravilhosas”, contou.

Ivonildes também disse que o filho ficou muito feliz com a oportunidade de votar. Ela o ajudou a registrar o voto na urna eletrônica.

“Ele ficou muito feliz por ter tido a oportunidade de votar. Eu ajudei ele a digitar, ele chamou a atenção do colégio inteiro”, relatou.

articles.title: Prince William: Knighthood for Sir Kevin Sinfield 'easiest decision anyone's had to make'
articles.summary: The rugby league star is "gold dust" and "should have been Sir Kevin years ago," says the Prince of Wales.
articles.body:
The Prince of Wales has said awarding a knighthood to rugby league star Sir Kevin Sinfield "was probably the easiest decision anyone's ever had to make".

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Prince William spoke about his personal admiration for Sir Kevin, who recently completed seven ultra marathons in seven days .

It was his latest endurance challenge to raise money for Motor Neurone Disease (MND) charities following the death of his friend and former team-mate, Rob Burrow, from the condition in 2024.

"I think frankly he should have been Sir Kevin years ago," said Prince William.

"What Kevin does, is he can bind and glue communities together by being that leader. The more Kevs we have in this country the better."

The Prince and Princess of Wales were in Wakefield in West Yorkshire last month to see for themselves just how gruelling the seven ultramarathon challenge was.

William and Catherine surprised Sir Kevin as he completed the third of the marathons.

"I don't know how he keeps going, I'm worried about his knees, I'm worried about his hips. The guy is just a machine," Prince William told the BBC.

"He's a top bloke, really nice guy, good, honest, kind, decent northerner and I love that about Kevin, that there is no ego with him. He is what you get."

Rob Burrow's MND diagnosis changed a relationship between team-mates into a public campaign to raise awareness.

Sir Kevin supported Rob and his family through the difficult progression of the disease, becoming an important fundraiser for the MND community.

"That lack of ego is really important in a world that everyone wants to show how amazing they all are… Kevin does it very quietly very subtly," explained the prince.

Prince William also told BBC Breakfast about writing to Rob Burrow's wife, Lindsey, and children, Macy, Maya and Jackson, after Rob's death. He said he was in awe of how Lindsey had coped with such quiet dignity.

He wrote the letter as a member of the Royal Family but also as someone who understood the anguish of losing a parent.

"Everyone grieves differently and every circumstance is different so you need to take your time over it," he said. "It's always better to say something around grief than it is to ignore it."

In November last year, I watched Prince William officially open the Rob Burrow Centre for Motor Neurone Disease at Seacroft Hospital in Leeds alongside the Burrow family.

The facility is dedicated to medical and holistic patient care as well as research into the condition. It was a deeply moving day for everyone there - but one filled with optimism.

Sinfield completes final ultramarathon challenge

Rob Burrow would be proud of knighthood - Sinfield

"It was very emotional actually and, for me, doing personal, emotional work is more fulfilling," the prince said.

"For Lindsey, Rob and the family to ask me to come up and open the centre was not only very personally rewarding for me but really important that that circle was closed, and I really wanted to honour that."

In the BBC Breakfast interview, the prince also praised the courage and impact of the Scottish rugby union player, Doddie Weir, who did so much to raise awareness of MND before his death from the disease in 2022 .

And there was also additional praise for William's aunt, the Princess Royal Anne, who has supported the MND community for many years.

Royal duty can be formal, even distant at times, but the story of Rob Burrow, his family and his friend Sir Kevin has clearly made an impact on a future King.

"He's a very kind, caring, human being but he's still a lunatic. How he manages all these things I don't know. He's gold dust he really is… if you could bottle it up and sell it, it would be priceless."

articles.title: Kylian Mbappé, 28 años, sobre su desayuno: "Empiezo el día con dos huevos duros acompañados de aguacate o mantequilla de almendras"
articles.standfirst: El astro francés fue la estrella del Clásico con un doblete
articles.summary: El astro francés fue la estrella del Clásico con un doblete
articles.body: Este lunes, 26 de octubre, Mbappé puede ser una de las personas más felices del mundo. El jugador francés definió el Clásico con un doblete y acercó al Real Madrid a tres puntos a LaLiga. Además, este mismo día podría recibir el que sería su primer Balón de Oro. Todo esto no sería posible si mantuviese un estado de forma excelso cada vez que salta al terreno de juego. Para mantener este estado físico durante los nueve meses que suele durar la competición, la alimentación es un pilar básico para cualquier jugador del mundo, pero más para Mbappé, dado su estilo de juego. Según el medio Muy Kitchen, hay diversos alimentos que nunca faltan en la dieta del capitán de la selección francesa. Y es que él los considera claves para llevar a cabo sus entrenamientos. El gran secreto de su físico puede ser el desayuno. Mbappé suele seguir siempre la misma rutina alimentaria: empieza el día con dos huevos duros acompañados de aguacate o mantequilla de almendras. Este menú te ayuda a recoger toda la energía y las proteínas necesarias para afrontar el día. Y en el Camp Nou, lo volvió a demostrar. A sus 28 años, el jugador galo sigue demostrando que se cuida al máximo en su apartado físico. Han pasado ya ocho años desde que deslumbró en el Mundial de Rusia de 2018. Considerado por la mayoría como uno de los tres mejores jugadores del mundo, la velocidad, potencia y resistencia siguen siendo las claves de su juego a pesar de rozar la treintena. La alimentación es una de las bases fundamentales de los futbolistas profesionales a día de hoy. Muchos tienen chefs privados, además de que los nutricionistas de los clubes les proporcionan dietas específicas dependiendo de su estilo de juego y gasto energético.

articles.title: Jordan arrests three suspects in deadly church attack
articles.summary: Suspects refuse to surrender and attack security forces, who return fire, wound and arrest them, authorities say.
articles.body:
Security forces have arrested three ⁠armed suspects in Jordan after days of searching for the attackers who killed eight people and wounded dozens at a church in Jordan’s Karak governorate, state media report.

The suspects were located on Monday while hiding in an abandoned house in the village of Al-Jadeeda in Karak, Jordan’s Public Security Directorate said.

They refused to surrender and attacked security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three after wounding them, the directorate said in a statement published on state media.

A Jordanian government source told Al Jazeera that the attackers sustained serious injuries during the confrontation with the security forces.

One of the suspects was in a critical condition as a result of the injuries sustained during the fighting, which lasted for about three hours, the source said.

No casualties were reported among security personnel, and a search of the site yielded firearms and live ammunition, according to Jordan’s Petra News Agency.

“Terrorism has no place among us,” the directorate said, adding that the ⁠suspects had met their “just fate” while not mentioning any specific affiliated groups.

In a statement posted on X early on Monday, Government Communication Minister Mohammad Momani commended the efforts of security forces involved in what he called a successful joint operation. Momani confirmed that all three suspects were injured and taken into custody following fighting after they refused to surrender.

On Friday, three gunmen opened fire at a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud in Karak, about ‌120km (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman, killing eight people and injuring 40, according to Jordan’s Ministry of Health.

Of the injured, 27 remained in hospital on Monday. The director of Prince Ali Military Hospital in the city of Karak said one person was in critical condition after undergoing surgery.

Karak is home to many members of Jordan’s Christian minority, which makes up about 300,000 of the country’s 11.5 million people.

King Abdullah II said those behind the attack would face the “harshest penalties” as he offered his condolences to the victims’ families. He has ordered a review of the country’s security procedures for responding to attacks.

Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya added that authorities were reviewing the circumstances that ‌lead ‌young people to embrace violence and would hold accountable anyone found to have participated in the attack.

articles.title: What happens when you eat a banana before working out?
articles.summary: Are you someone who is always looking for something to eat before you hit the gym and bananas are the only option to go for?
articles.body: Are you someone who is always looking for something to eat before you hit the gym and bananas are the only option to go for? Then you must sit back and read on! Well, consuming a banana before physical activity alters metabolic preparation, muscle function, and post-workout recovery. Far from being a simple natural snack, bananas provide a precise combination of rapidly digestible carbohydrates, essential electrolytes, and bioactive compounds that directly interact with physical exercise demands. Here’s all you need to know about it…All about carbs and absorptionsAs per a study by Appalachian State University Human Performance Laboratory, it was mentioned that during high-intensity training, muscles depend heavily on available glucose for energy. A medium banana contains roughly 27 grams of carbohydrates, comprising sucrose, glucose, and fructose. This specific natural sugar mix gives an advantage when it comes to how the cells take in the sugar. Glucose gets into the cells in the intestines using a transport system called the sodium-glucose cotransporter 1 or SGLT1. Fructose uses a system called GLUT5. Because these sugar molecules use paths to get into the body, the body can take in and release energy more smoothly than if it was only getting one type of sugar. The ripeness of the fruit affects how fast the energy is taken in. A banana that is ripe and has spots has mostly simple sugars that break down quickly. This kind of banana gives energy that's easy to use when eaten 30 to 45 minutes before working out. On the other hand, a greener banana is more resistant. starch. This kind of starch takes longer to break down. This can cause digestive problems if eaten too close to when someone is exercising.Bananas vs sports drinksThe physiological impact of bananas on exercise performance was examined in landmark studies conducted by Dr. David Nieman at the Appalachian State University Human Performance Laboratory. Researchers further evaluated trained cyclists undergoing intense, long-distance trials while consuming either bananas or a 6 percent carbohydrate sports beverage. The data published in PLOS ONE demonstrated that bananas provided equal support to athletic performance, blood glucose levels, and perceived exertion compared to manufactured sports drinks.Beyond equal performance energy, bananas altered post-exercise recovery markers. Cyclists consuming bananas showed significant reductions in COX-2 mRNA expression, a key genetic driver of systemic inflammation, along with improved cellular antioxidant capacity compared to those drinking standard sugar solutions. Balance and neuromuscular functionPotassium is the main salt inside cells that helps nerve signals travel and keeps cell fluids balanced. One banana gives about 422 milligrams of potassium, which is about 10 percent of what a person needs each day.When you exercise hard, potassium quickly moves from muscle cells into the blood. This can make muscles tired. Increase the chance of cramps during long workouts. Eating potassium before exercise keeps blood levels steady while you work out. It helps keep cells in the state and lets muscles contract in the right order. Bananas give vitamin B6 called pyridoxine, and provide more than 20 percent of the daily amount a person should take. Vitamin B6 works as a helper for the enzyme glycogen phosphorylase, which breaks down stored muscle glycogen into energy during effort.Optimizing workout timingTo get the best benefit and stay comfortable, eat a fully yellow ripe banana about 30 to 60 minutes before you exercise. This window lets the stomach finish emptying while preventing a drop in blood sugar that can happen when insulin kicks in at the start of training. Adding a cup of coffee gives caffeine that can boost endurance, and it does not slow digestion. Do not add heavy fats or very dense protein right before you exercise because a lot of fat slows stomach emptying and takes away from the fast carbs the banana provides.Post-workout shiftEating a banana after you work out changes its job from giving energy to helping cells recover quickly. After work muscle cells become more sensitive to insulin. This lets them pull glucose from the blood fast and refill their glycogen stores. The natural sugars in bananas such as sucrose, glucose, and fructose, can cause a rise in insulin that acts like a gatekeeper pushing glucose straight into muscle tissues for quick rebuilding. Also, if you eat a banana with a protein source after exercise, the two work together. The bananas' antioxidants and natural dopamine help lower muscle soreness and inflammation, while the amino acids from protein fix tissue damage.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: People living past 100 in one tiny village share 3 daily habits
articles.summary: National Geographic's potential blue zone in Sardinia's Bolotana has 10 centenarians among 2,262 residents, and their plant-based diet holds secrets.
articles.body: National Geographic researchers believe they may have discovered a new "blue zone." A blue zone is a geographic region where residents show unusually high rates of longevity and survival into old age. The newest blue zone candidate is a small village called Bolotana, located on the Italian island of Sardinia. In a 2024 snapshot, 10 of the village's 2,262 residents were at least 100 years old, according to National Geographic — roughly 10 times the Sardinian average and 11 times the U.S. average. PEOPLE WHO LIVE TO 100 HAVE 3 DRINKS IN COMMON, LONGEVITY EXPERT SAYS A team of researchers, including Dan Buettner — founder of Blue Zones, a company focused on longevity, and a National Geographic Fellow — set out to investigate Bolotana’s exceptional lifespan. The findings were published in Frontiers in Aging. Buettner highlighted three lifestyle habits that are common among Bolotana’s long-lived residents. "Here, men are participating more, and that could explain why women are doing better." The study did not establish that these habits directly cause longevity, but researchers are examining how the village’s environment and traditions may contribute to its unusually high survival rates. "The international team of demographers, their population scientists … were able to examine the birth records, death records and baptismal records and see that this is probably the richest, most complete data on centenarians in the world," Buettner told Fox News Digital. AMERICA'S LIFESPAN HAS DOUBLED SINCE 1776 — EXPERTS REVEAL WHAT CHANGED "For those of us who want to make it into our 90s and 100s in full health, this place does it better than anyplace else in the world." The strongest longevity advantage appeared among Bolotana’s women, who ranked second only to Hong Kong for life expectancy at age 70 and survival from age 70 to 100. What sets Bolotana apart The original Sardinian blue zone was identified in the late 1990s and formally described in research published around 2000. Located in the mountainous region roughly 68 miles from Bolotana, it is known for unusually strong male longevity, according to Buettner. Although Bolotana remains partly pastoral, it is also an agricultural community. Buettner suggested that this may mean men spend more time at home helping with household responsibilities, potentially reducing the burden on women. "In the original blue zone in the highlands, the [women] worried about the finances and raising children and the leaky roof," he said. "They're all alone. Here, men are participating more, and that could explain why women are doing better, because they're only bearing half the stress load instead of almost all of it." Buettner believes the village’s strong social connections may be one factor behind the women’s longevity, although the study did not establish a cause. GEORGIA WOMAN CELEBRATES 112TH BIRTHDAY, REVEALS HER SECRET TO A LONG LIFE "We see women gathering in the library, baking bread together, making sweets together and going to church together," he said. "So, you see a much more socially connected society among the women in Bolotana than in the other blue zones." As in many parts of Italy, Bolotana has a strong Catholic tradition. Buettner said church attendance may provide residents with faith, social connection and a sense of belonging. "It’s a sense of community, but it's also people proactively understanding that sitting down with a friend and talking about your troubles and your day with somebody who cares about you is a much more powerful drug than a pharmaceutical," Buettner said. "The human species has shown this over and over, and Bolotana is a perfect example." The Bolotana diet Diet varies among blue zones, but Bolotana’s traditional fare is largely plant-based, with a focus on beans, vegetables, wheat, olives and olive oil, along with some cheese and meat. DOCTOR'S 10 RULES FOR LIVING LONGER, CELEBRATING MORE BIRTHDAYS AND MAKING EXTRA YEARS COUNT "About 90% of a centenarian's diet has been all plant-based," Buettner said. "Not protein, by the way. These aren't protein loaders. These are complex carbohydrate loaders." A Bolotanese breakfast might consist of a piece of bread or cheese with local olives and a cup of coffee. Lunch, the biggest meal of the day that starts in the early afternoon, is "almost always" a minestrone soup made with locally grown seasonal vegetables and lots of beans. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "Beans are the cornerstone of the longevity diet here," Buettner said. "Garbanzo beans, lentil beans, pinto beans, cannellini beans — these are really the all-star of the diet." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Traditionally, residents ate meat about five times per month, usually as a celebratory food. In the highlands, people traditionally cooked with lard, Buettner said, while Bolotana residents use olive oil from ancient trees. Researchers are studying whether the oil’s unusually high levels of odd-chain fatty acids could be relevant to longevity. ‘Not chasing’ longevity Bolotana residents are not deliberately pursuing longer lives, the longevity researcher noted. The region has little emphasis on gym culture or biohacking. "These are real humans with an average set of genes," Buettner said. "These aren’t superhumans with superhuman discipline or better genes." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "They’re not chasing longevity," he added. "It is the product of their environment." Because Bolotana’s streets are steep and residents rarely drive within town, they typically walk to shops, cafés, workplaces and friends’ homes, Buettner said. "It’s this sort of unconscious walking that’s far more important for longevity than going to the gym." Buettner said Bolotana is an example of how daily routines and surroundings can encourage movement without requiring residents to schedule formal exercise. Residents of walkable American communities have a three- to five-year life-expectancy advantage over those in less-walkable areas, he said. "If we want a healthier America, we have to start thinking about shaping our neighborhoods and our cities so people can unconsciously move and not rely on heaping another obligation on their busy lives to remember to go to the gym," the expert said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Most of the things that lead to Bolotana longevity are also pleasant and make the journey a joy," he added.

articles.title: After seeing patients lose their sight while waiting for treatment, Surat doctor Bhavin Patel takes eye care to Gujarat’s villages, with over 30,000 free surgeries and nearly 40 monthly screening camps
articles.summary: For some patients, the biggest barrier to saving their eyesight is not the treatment itself.
articles.body: For some patients, the biggest barrier to saving their eyesight is not the treatment itself. It is reaching a doctor before the condition becomes too serious. In parts of Gujarat, people living in remote villages may delay eye check-ups because of travel costs, limited awareness or difficulty accessing specialists. By the time they reach a hospital, a condition that could have been treated earlier may have already caused lasting damage.This is a problem that Dr Bhavin Patel, a retina specialist in Surat, has spent years trying to address. Instead of waiting for patients to find their way to a hospital, he has helped build an outreach system that takes eye screening into villages and brings patients who need treatment to Surat. According to figures shared in the original report by The Better India, the initiative has conducted more than 30,000 free surgeries and organises nearly 40 screening camps each month. Behind these numbers is an approach built around one simple idea: eye care must reach people before it is too late.The real problem begins before patients reach a hospitalDr Patel began his medical practice in Surat in 2008, starting with a clinic focused on retinal care. Over time, he encountered patients whose conditions had worsened because they could not access timely treatment. Some had ignored blurred vision, while others struggled to afford specialist consultations or travel to larger hospitals. For patients with serious retinal conditions, delays can have lasting consequences.The scale of preventable vision loss in India makes early diagnosis particularly important. A national survey conducted between 2015 and 2019 found that 92.9% of blindness and 97.4% of visual impairment among people aged 50 and above were attributable to avoidable causes. Cataract was responsible for 66.2% of blindness in this age group. The findings, published in PLOS ONE, underline the importance of accessible screening, timely treatment and follow-up care. For Dr Patel, the challenge was not simply to treat more patients. It was to identify people who needed help before their conditions became more difficult to manage.From village screenings to treatment in SuratThe outreach programme developed around Swami Vivekanand Netra Mandir, the eye hospital Dr Patel established in Surat. The associated non-profit trust was established in 2022, according to its official website. Its approach begins in villages, where local volunteers help identify residents who may need eye examinations. Screening teams check vision and look for signs of cataracts, retinal disorders and other eye conditions. People who need basic assistance, such as spectacles, can receive support through outreach services. Those who require surgery or specialist treatment are referred to the hospital in Surat. Transport is arranged for eligible patients, helping reduce the difficulties of travelling long distances.The programme also works with local community networks to encourage residents to attend screening camps. Familiar locations and trusted volunteers can make it easier for people to seek care, especially when they have limited information about eye diseases. According to the reported figures, the team conducts nearly 40 camps each month and around 1,000 free cataract surgeries monthly. The trust's official also lists community screening camps, school eye checks, spectacle distribution, treatment for premature babies with retinopathy of prematurity and vocational training for visually impaired people.When treatment restores more than eyesightThe impact of accessible eye care can extend beyond a medical outcome. For someone who depends on daily wages, poor vision can make earning a living difficult. For families, caring for a person who has lost their sight may also bring financial pressure and changes to everyday responsibilities. The original report by The Better India described the experience of Nathuram Makwana, a construction worker who lost vision in both eyes following a workplace injury. When he eventually received treatment, the improvement was limited, but even being able to perceive some light and shadows offered a measure of hope. His experience also encouraged him to advise others not to delay seeking medical help.Another case involved Vihana, a premature baby diagnosed with retinopathy of prematurity. Her family had already spent a substantial amount seeking treatment. After reaching Dr Patel's hospital, she underwent surgery on both eyes. Her father said the treatment brought relief to a family that had feared she might lose her sight. Such stories also highlight an important distinction: treatment cannot always restore vision completely. Outcomes depend on the condition, its severity and how early it is treated. That is why screening and timely referral remain essential.Building independence after vision lossDr Patel's work also addresses what happens when sight cannot be fully restored. Losing vision can affect a person's confidence, mobility, employment and ability to manage daily tasks independently. The trust's rehabilitation programme offers training in computer use, smartphone skills and mobility. The aim is to help visually impaired people build practical abilities and prepare for work rather than leaving them without support after treatment. This approach reflects a wider understanding of eye care. Medical treatment may address a condition, but rehabilitation can help people adapt, regain confidence and participate more independently in everyday life.The challenge of preventable blindness remains significant, particularly for people who struggle to reach healthcare services. By combining village screening, hospital treatment and rehabilitation, Dr Patel's initiative seeks to address several stages of that challenge. Its larger lesson is that healthcare cannot depend entirely on patients finding their way to specialists. Sometimes, the first and most important step is taking care closer to the communities that need it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A Dietitian’s ‘Perfect Fall Snack’ Is Packed With Plant Protein and Healthy Fats
articles.summary: Try this dietitian-approved recipe for a snack that’s packed with plant-based protein, fiber, omega-3s and more. Made with apple and spices, it’s a tasty treat.
articles.body: One of the most delicious ways to enjoy warm fall flavors is also one of the most nutritious. With plant-based protein, fiber and omega-3s, this dietitian-approved recipe is a tasty, energizing treat with major health benefits. This filling, energizing recipe is a favorite of Natalie Rizzo, registered dietitian and TODAY nutrition editor. She recommends grabbing some before a workout or as a sweet treat after a meal. Nutrition Tip of the Day: Try This No-Bake Fall Snack to Get More Plant-Based Protein Rizzo’s No-Bake Apple Spiced Energy Bites are a delicious autumnal snack that packs plant protein, fiber and more into a small, tasty package. “As a dietitian, I’m always looking for satisfying snacks that are easy to make and keep me full until my next meal,” she says. “These apple-spiced energy bites check all those boxes, and they’re the perfect fall snack.” In this snack, you’ll find oats, almond butter, apple chips, dates and delicious spices. But the starting ingredient is hemp seeds, Rizzo says, which are small but mighty. Why It Matters “Each bite offers a balance of nutrients,” Rizzo says. The oats provide complex carbohydrates and fiber, both of which support digestion and give you some lasting energy. “The almond butter adds plant-based protein and heart-healthy unsaturated fats,” she continues, “while the dates and dried apples provide natural sweetness and additional fiber.” Then there’s the hemp seeds, which provide more healthy fats and are a plant protein powerhouse. A 3-tablespoon serving of hemp seeds contains nearly 10 grams of protein, making them one of the top high-protein seeds. And a serving of Rizzo’s energy bites (3 pieces) will net you 7 grams of plant-based protein. Together, these nutrients will keep you feeling full, satisfied and energized. They’re perfect for a quick snack, an evening treat or a pre- or post-workout bite. How to Get Started To make Rizzo’s no-bake energy bites, you’ll just need a few ingredients, a food processor, a mixing bowl and a little patience. You’ll start by blitzing apple chips, oats, dates and almond butter in the food processor. Then you’ll add the hemp seeds and your spices to the mixture and form them into balls. The mixture comes together in about 10 minutes, and the energy bites will firm up after about an hour in the fridge. articles.title: Medieval hospital built for victims of feared disease gives up long-buried secrets
articles.summary: A three-day dig at Lincoln's Hospital of the Holy Innocents in England uncovered small structures that may have served as private quarters for leprosy patients.
articles.body: Archaeologists in England have uncovered new remains at one of the country's oldest and largest medieval leprosy hospitals, hundreds of years after the disease ravaged communities across Britain. The recent excavation, reported by British news agency Jam Press, centered on South Common in Lincoln, a historic English city roughly 140 miles north of London. The site was once home to the Hospital of the Holy Innocents, which was founded between the late 11th and early 12th centuries. MYSTERIOUS SETTLEMENT DISCOVERED AFTER RESIDENTS SEEMINGLY PACKED UP AND VANISHED During a three-day excavation, archaeologists from the British television program "Time Team" uncovered traces of medieval walls and possible living quarters. The hospital operated for nearly 500 years, housing up to 20 leprosy patients at a time, officials said. The findings build on an excavation that took place last year, when volunteers unearthed walls, building surfaces and artifacts linked to the former hospital. This time, researchers identified traces of small, square features that may have served as individual living quarters or enclosed yards for patients. The structures have never been excavated before, researchers said, according to Jam Press. SHOCKING DISCOVERY OF ANCIENT BONES TURNS COUPLE'S KITCHEN RENOVATION INTO 'CRIME SCENE' The findings offer a rare glimpse into how leprosy patients may have lived during the Middle Ages, including who could afford to receive care. "You'd need to have resources to get in here," professor Carenza Lewis of the University of Lincoln said, according to Jam Press. "If you had enough money and could buy your way into a leper hospital, it's a bit like getting a place in a private care home or something like that." Historical documents suggest the hospital accommodated up to 20 patients, who may have lived in separate structures with small yards, Lewis said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "We know that they had little sorts of curtilages [enclosed plots of land], which implies they're separate little buildings, little houses with a little yard, perhaps," she said. Leprosy, also known as Hansen's disease, is a chronic bacterial infection that primarily affects the skin, nerves and eyes. Although the disease can cause severe disfigurement if left untreated, it is curable with antibiotics and still exists today. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The excavation is part of a three-year research project led by Anglia Ruskin University, which aims to learn more about the people who lived, worked and died at the medieval hospital. Leprosy is curable with antibiotics and still exists today. Tim Taylor, the creator of "Time Team," said the site could reveal more about Lincoln's archaeological past. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Lincoln has an extraordinary archaeological story, and this site promises to give us the opportunity to uncover a fascinating part of it," Taylor said, Jam Press reported. The findings come after a similar discovery last year in York, England, where a sinkhole in a city street exposed the remains of one of northern England's largest medieval hospitals. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The remains were believed to belong to St. Leonard's Hospital and date back to the 12th or 13th century.

articles.title: Matthew Perry’s Sister Says This Reframing Made it ‘Easier to Love Him’ Through Substance Use Disorder
articles.summary: Matthew Perry’s sister Mia Perry Bowick remembered him in a documentary and on TODAY and shared how she learned to understand his substance use disorder.
articles.body: Matthew Perry’s life is being remembered in a three-part documentary series by the people who knew him best, including his sister Mia Perry Bowick. “Yes, he was just that wonderful,” Bowick said during an appearance on TODAY Oct. 26. “All of those warm, comforting feelings you get from him, he gave them to his family and friends.” The “Friends” star died of acute effects of ketamine at 54 in October 2023. Perry had been open about his decadeslong struggle with addiction. He estimated in his memoir, which published one year before his death, that he spent $7 million on efforts to get sober. Bowick said in the documentary, out Oct. 27 on Netflix, that her brother’s struggle impacted her career path. She became a licensed psychotherapist working in substance use treatment. Bowick said when Perry first started telling people about addiction, there was “very little nuance or understanding about what substance use disorder is.” “I only had information from the D.A.R.E. program. It’s kind of very black and white — if you use a drug, you’re going to die,” she said. Bowick said she wished she understood at the time “it was a disease.” “When you can think of it from the disease perspective, it’s a lot easier to understand why they can’t stop, and it’s helpful for the families to not take it as personally that they can’t stop,” she said. “As we learned more and more about what’s happening to him, it was easier to love him through it, rather than try to control what was happening,” she added. Perry wrote in his memoir that he had a near death experience in 2019 after his colon burst from opioid overuse. He also said his heart stopped at a rehab facility in Switzerland. Perry had been receiving ketamine infusion therapy before his death “to ease pain and help with depression,” he wrote in his memoir. According to an autopsy, his last ketamine infusion therapy treatment had been a week and a half before his death, which could not have been the ketamine in his system when he died. Five individuals, including Perry’s assistant Kenneth Iwamasa and Jasveen Sangha, nicknamed the “Ketamine Queen, were charged in connection with Perry’s fatal drug overdose, per a press release from the U.S. Attorney’s Office, Central District of California. Prosecutors alleged their roles in distributing ketamine to Perry caused his death. Prosecutors said Perry was experiencing severe ketamine addiction and was injecting the drug six to eight times a day before his death. The actor sought out unsupervised doses and developed an “out of control” dependence on it, prosecutors said. If you or someone you know is struggling with an alcohol, drug or other substance use problem, call the free and confidential helpline of the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration at 1-800-662-HELP (1-800-662-4357), or visit findtreatment.gov.

articles.title: Vote now for the Bronson Battle Creek Girls Athlete of the Week for Oct. 19-24
articles.summary: Make your choice for Battle Creek Enquirer Athlete of the Week for girls sports, including athletes from Harper Creek, Lakeview, St. Philip. The poll closes...
articles.body:
BATTLE CREEK — Meet the most recent nominees for Battle Creek Enquirer Athletes of the Week, presented by Bronson Battle Creek Hospital.

Each week during the high school sports season, we will ask our readers to vote for the top performance of the week in all high school sports, taking a look at events from Monday-Saturday. In 2026, the Enquirer will have an Athlete of the Week for boys sports and an Athlete of the Week for girls sports.

Make sure to vote early and often for your pick, as the winner will be featured in an Athlete of the Week spotlight story in the Sunday edition of the Enquirer. Fans can vote for their favorite athlete until 5 p.m., Wednesday, Oct. 28.

Nominees for Bronson Battle Creek Athlete of the Week for girls sports

Mylee Grimm reached a career milestone for the St. Philip volleyball team as the senior reached 1,500 digs. Along the way, Grimm helped St. Philip win a league title with an undefeated record in the conference as the Tigers are ranked in the state in Division 4.

Lakeview closed out its regular season dual season with a 114-61 win over Kalamazoo Central. Senior Mia Schuemann helped the Spartans to the one-sided win with a first place in the 100 breaststroke as well as being part of two first-place relay teams, winning the 200 freestyle relay and the 200 medley relay.

Freshman Lucy Schwartz provided key depth as Harper Creek won the Interstate 8 Conference team title in girls cross country. Harper Creek had five runners in the top 11 in the conference championship meet with Schwartz finishing seventh in a time of 20:39.

Senior Alivia Winer helped Lakeview clinch the Southwestern Michigan Athletic Conference championship in volleyball. The Spartans had already won the East Division title and then played West Division champ Stevensville-Lakeshore in a crossover match. Lakeview won in four to secure the overall conference title with Alivia Winer playing big with 17 assists and 16 digs.
